question: Food supplements contain vitamins, minerals, botanicals, probiotics and other substances sensitive to moisture, oxygen and light. Packaging, including blisters and sachets, is essential for maintaining the quality and safety of food supplements throughout their two-to-three-year shelf life.

Article 6(11) of the Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation1 exempts the immediate packaging of medicinal products and certain specialised foods from recyclability requirements, but excludes food supplements. Consequently, the same high-barrier blister packaging may remain permissible for a medicine but becomes non-compliant for a food supplement, despite comparable product-protection requirements.

Design-for-recycling criteria must be adopted by 1 January 2028, potentially leaving only 24 months before the compliance deadline, while product-specific stability testing alone can take 36 months. 1.
Why are food supplements not included in Article 6(11), despite comparable productprotection requirements?
How does the Commission expect manufacturers to achieve compliance by 2030 when the final criteria may only become available in 2028 and validation alone may take up to 36 months?

What concrete measures will the Commission take to safeguard consumer safety, product availability and the competitiveness of small and medium-sized enterprises, while preventing increased packaging and product waste, and in particular, how will it address the need for a targeted derogation until at least 2035 where no technically validated recyclable alternatives are available?

Regulation (EU) 2025/40 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 19 December 2024 on packaging and packaging waste, amending Regulation (EU) 2019/1020 and Directive (EU) 2019/904, and repealing Directive 94/62/EC, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2025/40/oj. 1
